title: The four riders (Revelation 6)
hookLine: conquest, war, famine and death ride out

cards: The Lamb takes the scroll and breaks the first seal. One of the living creatures says, like thunder, "Come and see."
A white horse comes out, its rider holding a bow, wearing a crown, going out "conquering, and to conquer." Second seal: a red horse, its rider given power "to take peace from the earth."
Third: a black horse, its rider holding scales. Fourth: a pale horse, "and his name that sat on him was Death." Readers have named them conquest, war, famine and death.
But a quieter moment in this chapter comes after the horses have gone.

teach.h: FOUR RIDERS: CONQUEST, WAR, FAMINE, DEATH.
teach.b: First, the riders. The red one is given a great sword, "that they should kill one another."
The black one carries scales, and a voice calls out prices: "A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine."
Grain is dear, while the oil and the wine are spared. The pale one is Death, "and Hell followed with him."
The white rider is argued over: plain conquest, or Christ, since a rider on a white horse returns later in the book.
Second, who opens the seals: the Lamb. Readers differ on what that means. Some see judgment.
Others see the world's own doings unveiled, with limits even on Death and Hell: power was given them "over the fourth part of the earth." Third, the fifth seal.
Under the altar, John sees the souls of those killed for the word of God, crying: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?"
It's the question of the Psalms: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" Scripture lets people ask God that out loud, in heaven itself. Fourth, the answer isn't an explanation.

teach.h: WHITE ROBES, AND A LITTLE REST.
teach.b: "White robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season." A robe, rest, and a question left open for now.
If that cry is your own tonight, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

how: Christians pray for places suffering war and famine in their own prayers and in the prayers of the people during services, and some churches pray in lament using the Psalms' cry of 'how long'.

o: four kings who will rule the world at the very end
conquest, war, famine and death, sent out as seals open
four angels who guard the four corners of the earth

p: to take peace from the earth
souls under the altar: how long?

s: Death and Hell are given power over the whole earth
"over the fourth part of the earth." not all of it.
the souls under the altar are scolded for asking how long
they're given white robes and told to rest a little season.
the cry of how long echoes the Psalms
Psalm 13:1: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?"

games.q: you're under the altar with those killed for the word of God. the riders have gone out. you've waited. what do you do?
o: stay silent; questions aren't allowed in heaven.
cry out: how long, O Lord?
games.why: they cry, "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" and they aren't silenced: they're given white robes and told to rest a little season.

practice: Bring one place of war or hunger to mind, just one, no flood of pictures, and hold it gently, the way you'd hold someone's hand in a hospital.
If you pray, name that place before God, or borrow the words from under the altar, how long, O Lord; if not, keep it in your attention for a few slow breaths and let it matter to you.

wordCard.voice: The four riders. Conquest, war, famine and death, released as the Lamb opens the seals; then, from under the altar: how long?

orig.note: Greek: pale, with a greenish tinge. the color of the fourth horse in Revelation 6:8.

carryVoice: Your line: how long? Even heaven makes room for that question, asked out loud. Until tomorrow.
